title: Beef and Broccoli Stir-fry
subtitle: Velveted beef with tender broccoli in a glossy oyster sauce
excerpt: Thin slices of beef are treated with bicarbonate of soda to tenderise them, then stir-fried with broccoli in a glossy oyster sauce. The technique is quick, the result is restaurant quality, and it works as a weeknight dinner with rice in under 30 minutes. Serves 4 in about 25 minutes.
sourceNotes: Beef with broccoli in oyster sauce is a dish rooted in Cantonese stir-fry tradition, where oyster sauce, developed in the late nineteenth century by Lee Kum Sheung in Guangdong province, became a central seasoning. The dish appears in various forms in Eileen Yin-Fei Lo's 'The Dim Sum Book' (Crown, 1982) and in Chinese-American cookbooks from the mid-twentieth century, where it became one of the most ordered dishes at Cantonese restaurants.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The beef can be velveted and left covered in the fridge for up to 2 hours before cooking.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Chinese technique in which raw protein is coated in a mixture of egg white, cornflour and sometimes bicarbonate of soda before cooking. The bicarbonate of soda raises the pH of the meat surface, which weakens the muscle fibres and produces a noticeably tender, silky texture after stir-frying.

A mixture of cornflour and cold water stirred together just before use. When added to a hot sauce it thickens it quickly to a glossy consistency. Always mix the slurry immediately before adding it to the pan, as the starch settles if left to stand.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and is ready in about 25 minutes once the beef has been
for 15 minutes. Most of that time is passive. The actual cooking takes less than 10 minutes, so have everything sliced and measured before the wok goes on the heat.

The bicarbonate of soda in the velvet marinade is the key step. Even a budget cut of beef will come out tender if left for 15 minutes. Rinse it off thoroughly before cooking or the beef will taste soapy. The
added at the end pulls the sauce together into a glossy coating that clings to each piece.

items.prepNote: cut into small florets, stalks peeled and sliced

content.text: Toss the {{beef-flank}} slices with {{bicarbonate-of-soda}}, {{cornflour}}, {{soy-sauce}} and oil. Mix well and leave for 15 minutes. Rinse the beef under cold running water, drain and pat dry. This step is important.
Mix the sauce ingredients together in a small bowl: {{oyster-sauce}}, soy sauce, {{sesame-oil}}, sugar and the cornflour slurry. Set aside.
Bring a pan of water to the boil. Blanch the {{broccoli}} for 2 minutes until bright green and just tender. Drain and set aside.

Heat a wok over a high heat until smoking. Add 1 tablespoon of the cooking oil, then add the beef in a single layer. Do not stir for 1 minute, allowing it to sear. Toss and cook for another 30 seconds. Remove to a plate.
Add the remaining oil to the wok, then fry the {{garlic}} and {{ginger}} for 30 seconds. Add the broccoli and toss for 1 minute.
Return the beef to the wok. Pour in the sauce mixture, stir everything together and cook for 1 minute until the sauce is glossy and thick. Serve immediately with steamed rice.

items.cause: The bicarbonate of soda was not rinsed off properly
items.fix: Rinse the velveted beef under cold running water for a full minute, then pat it completely dry before stir-frying.

items.symptom: The beef is steaming rather than searing
items.cause: The wok is not hot enough or there is too much beef in the wok at once
items.fix: Get the wok smoking before adding the oil. Cook the beef in two batches if needed, letting each piece make full contact with the wok surface.

items.symptom: The sauce is thin and watery
items.cause: The cornflour slurry was not mixed before adding, or the wok temperature dropped too much
items.fix: Stir the slurry just before adding it and keep the heat high. The sauce should thicken within 30 to 45 seconds.

content.text: Beef and broccoli is made at home across China and in Chinese-American restaurants, where the sauce is often sweeter. The key is the beef. Velveted sirloin or rump stays tender at high heat. Cheaper cuts toughen quickly in a wok. Do not overcook the broccoli; it should still have bite.
